full_text:
The UK is set to enjoy a bright and sunny weekend after a spell of showery weather earlier this week.
Although temperatures will be warm, with highs of 24C in London, it is still a long way off from the record breaking heatwaves so far this year.
The rain and cooler temperatures were welcomed after back-to-back heatwaves left the ground hard and dry with 70 per cent of England and Wales in drought.
Provisional Met Office data shows that the UK’s mean temperature for meteorological summer so far is currently at 16.48C – that is 1.88C above the 1991 to 2020 average temperature. England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far, 2.46C above average.
The remainder of August would need to be 1.41C below the summer average for England to equal its current warmest summer on record, also set in 2025.
But will there be another dry and sunny spell this summer?
What does the long range forecast say?
Looking ahead, the Met Office’s long range weather forecast predicts that the changeable weather is likely to continue.
From early next week the south of England is forecast to see more unsettled weather as longer spells of rain spread north across many parts of the UK.
In the days before the start of September some heavy bursts and thunderstorms are likely.
“Thereafter, it will likely remain changeable through the rest of August and into early September, with rainfall amounts probably above average for the time of year,” according to the Met Office.
But warm and hot spells are still possible, although they will likely be short lived, with temperatures sitting near average.
There will be some drier and more settled spells before an unsettled start to autumn.
At the start of September the Met Office predicts all areas will probably see a mixture of showers and dry weather.
While the beginning of September will bring varying temperatures by mid-September, there may be an increase in the extent of drier, more settled weather, especially in the south and east, according to forecasters.
What records have been broken this summer?
The Met Office said last week temperatures had reached 37.6C at Charlwood in Surrey, while at Wisley temperatures had hit 37.2C, and Kew Gardens in London had recorded a temperature of 38.1C – the highest temperature recorded in the UK this year.
A further 10 weather stations were at or above 36C, the provisional figures from the Met Office showed.
It makes 2026 the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold, as well as the first year with four days at 36C or above.
Before 2026, the UK had recorded 37C or higher on only six occasions.
It also extends 2026’s record-breaking run of days above 35C.
For four months in a row temperatures hit 35C in the UK on at least one day in May, June, July and now August.
July was also the driest month since records began in 1836 in both England and Wales, southern England alone had its driest calendar month ever on record.
By 15 July this year the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.
Why is the UK experiencing more heatwaves?
Climate change is making extremes such as heat and drought more intense and more likely.
The UK's weather is becoming warmer and wetter, and adverse weather events - heatwaves, flooding, extreme cold - are growing more frequent and intense. The last decade has been warmer than any previous decade on record, and summers we once considered exceptional are becoming the norm.
The Met Office explains that the UK is experiencing higher maximum temperatures and longer warm spells in recent years. Warm spells have seen their average length more than double – increasing from 5.3 days in 1961-90 to over 13 days in the decade 2008-2017.
But the outlook could get worse. A study by the Met Office Hadley Centre suggests the current chance of seeing days reaching 40C or more is extremely low. However, by 2100 under a high emissions scenario the UK could see 40 C days every three to four years.

The monsoon remains active over Madhya Pradesh, with heavy rain continuing in several districts. A strong weather system is active over Madhya Pradesh due to the monsoon trough, a cyclonic circulation and a low-pressure area. As a result, heavy rain has been lashing the eastern parts of the state for the past two days, and several rivers are in spate.
The weather department has issued an orange alert for extremely heavy rain in Seoni and Balaghat today. A heavy rain alert has also been issued for 12 districts, including Datia, Bhind, Niwari, Tikamgarh, Chhatarpur, Panna, Sagar and Damoh. Light to heavy rain is also expected in several other parts of the state.

The risk of forest fires on Sunday has been set at “red alert”, the forestry department said on Saturday.
Alongside the setting of the fire risk level, the department also issued a reminder that the lighting of a fire without a permit is a criminal offence punishable by up to 10 years in prison, a fine of €50,000, or both.
Lighting a fire to prepare food is only permitted in the barbecue areas of picnic sites.
The forestry department also warned people to be “especially careful” to avoid “actions and activities which would likely cause a fire”, including the use of agricultural machinery and welding tools.
Those who notice smoke or fire are encouraged to call the forestry department on 1407 or the fire brigade on 112 immediately.

UAE's NCM issues yellow alert for rain, a day after unstable weather seen in Abu Dhabi
- PUBLISHED: Sat 22 Aug 2026, 12:54 PM
UAE's National Centre of Meteorology has issued a yellow alert for rain, active till 9pm today (August 22), in some parts of the country, including Al Ain, which saw heavy rains on Friday.
The yellow alert warns of a chance that convective clouds may form — these are associated with rainfall. The alert also cautions residents of fresh to strong winds, resulting in blowing dust and sand, and reduced horizontal visibility.
The NCM said the weather conditions are expected to affect some eastern, southern and western areas, extending to parts of the country's interior. Take a look at where the yellow alerts have been issued
Stay up to date with the latest news. Follow KT on WhatsApp Channels.
Weather forecast today
According to UAE's NCM, the weather will be fair to partly cloudy today. Convective clouds are likely to form towards the eastern and southern parts of the country by afternoon.
Temperatures are expected to rise gradually, with highs of 46°C in Abu Dhabi, 44°C in Dubai and Sharjah, while lows across the three emirates will be around 33°C.
It will be humid by night and Sunday morning over some coastal areas.
Humidity levels are expected to range from 15 to 65 per cent in Abu Dhabi, 20 to 60 per cent in Dubai and 15 to 55 per cent in Sharjah.
Light to moderate winds will blow from the southeast to northeast, freshening at times and reaching speeds of up to 50kmph.
Heavy rain on Friday
On August 21, heavy rain, thunder and lightning was seen in some parts of Abu Dhabi. Trees and road signs could be seen shaking as residents in cars drove through water-lined streets.
The weather conditions also prompted precautionary measures across the capital. Abu Dhabi City Municipality temporarily closed all parks, recreational facilities and affiliated beaches and suspended events until further notice. Al Ain City Municipality also announced the temporary closure of parks.
Al Ain later said that its parks have reopened while Abu Dhabi announced the reopening of its parks, recreational facilities, and affiliated beaches.
The municipality said the measures were taken as a precaution to protect residents and ensure public safety amid fluctuating weather and heavy rainfall in several parts of Abu Dhabi.
